text.title: Content Audit Basics Decision Tree
text.summary: Routes on corpus size and whether a URL-changing migration is already scheduled, what data can be joined per URL, and what the decision column is about to do — to a full audit, an inventory or window fix, a decision-column correction, or a skip.

decision-tree.root-question: How many URLs are in scope, and is a URL-changing migration or replatform already scheduled?

branch.when: the site is under roughly 50 URLs

conclusion.verdict: skip: one sitting reading every page beats building a rubric — at this size every page is already in someone's head

branch.when: a replatform or IA change that rewrites URLs is already scheduled

conclusion.verdict: skip or re-aim: audit against the destination information architecture, or the keep/delete list is keyed to URLs that will not exist and gets applied by mistake anyway

branch.when: a few hundred URLs or more, with no URL-changing migration scheduled and no inventory built yet
branch.question: What data can actually be joined per URL before scoring starts?

branch.when: analytics has no conversion or goal events configured, so entrances are the only metric available

conclusion.verdict: skip until goals are instrumented: half the decision evidence does not exist and every delete would rest on pageviews alone

branch.when: analytics and Search Console are available, but the URL list would be assembled by walking the site navigation

conclusion.verdict: generate the inventory from a crawler export joined to the XML sitemap and server-log or analytics hits, and report the orphan set explicitly — a nav-walk is structurally blind to the retired and campaign URLs the audit exists to find

branch.when: crawl, analytics and Search Console join cleanly, but the metrics window on hand is 90 days or a single quarter

conclusion.verdict: widen the window to at least 12 months and state it on the artefact; flag pages published in the two most recent quarters as too new to judge and exclude them from delete eligibility

branch.when: crawl plus at least 12 months of entrances, conversions, impressions and clicks join per row, and the rubric's criteria, weights and keep/update threshold are written down before the first URL is scored

conclusion.verdict: apply the full methodology: crawl-derived inventory with orphans, metric columns per row, rubric scoring, ROT labels with proof, and a decision column with redirect targets

branch.when: an inventory is already scored and the open question is what to do per URL
branch.question: What is about to be written into the decision column, and on what evidence?

branch.when: rows are getting delete or consolidate decisions while their traffic and conversion columns are empty

conclusion.verdict: hold those rows at quality-score only: the rubric scores the prose and deletion destroys traffic, and a thin page can hold the majority of a category's organic entrances

branch.when: deletes are queued with no redirect_target, and some of those URLs carry referring domains or external referral entrances

conclusion.verdict: attach a redirect_target, or an accept_404 flag with a written reason and a named sign-off on any row with inbound links — an unredirected removal discards the link equity and the referral traffic still flowing

branch.when: non-keep rows say update with no named defect, or carry no ROT label at all

conclusion.verdict: label each non-keep row Redundant, Outdated or Trivial with its proof field — duplicate cluster or competing URL, a named stale fact, or the metric below the declared threshold; the three labels are three different jobs with three different owners

branch.when: the scores came back unwelcome and someone proposes adjusting the weights or the threshold

conclusion.verdict: refuse the post-hoc change or open a new artefact_id and re-score every row; weights tuned after the scores are visible let the audit ratify the outcome the team already wanted
